source_defaults.notes: Named candidate answers to a common publisher questionnaire. Publication and recorded revision dates precede the primary. Candidate statistics, records and forecasts remain attributed claims, not independent findings.

statements.quote: It is time to add back publicly owned housing.
statements.claim: Calls for more publicly owned housing and incentives for collective ownership rather than relying only on market production.

statements.quote: invest in short- and medium-term public housing
statements.claim: Supports short- and medium-term public housing, tenant protections, rent-control measures and right-of-first-refusal legislation.

statements.quote: fought for and won Inclusionary Zoning mandates
statements.claim: Expresses support for inclusionary zoning and describes neighborhood mandates, while saying inclusionary zoning alone is insufficient. The claimed unit totals are not independently certified.

statements.quote: pass inclusionary zoning measures citywide
statements.claim: Calls for citywide inclusionary zoning. His criticism of the number of homes produced is a campaign claim, not this study's verified housing inventory.

statements.quote: We can double the budget for Parks and Recreation.
statements.claim: Proposes doubling Parks and Recreation funding, adding youth supports and addressing household needs as part of violence prevention.

statements.quote: universal child care, before- and after-school programs
statements.claim: Proposes childcare, school programs, mental-health supports and community resources as violence-prevention investments.

statements.quote: desk jobs that could be filled by civilians
statements.claim: Would shift desk and other non-police tasks to civilians so officers can focus on work requiring police; this is not a proposal to eliminate every police function.

statements.quote: officer recruitment and retention
statements.claim: Emphasizes recruitment, retention, diversity, pay and officer wellness; also endorses partnerships with social workers and mental-health professionals.

statements.quote: cannot be achieved through private ownership of the Shuman Center
statements.claim: Opposes private ownership of the Shuman Center and seeks retained county authority and oversight.

statements.quote: Certainly, it must remain a public entity. We must not privatize.
statements.claim: Opposes privatizing Shuman and favors studying its future with judges, social workers, psychologists and community members.

statements.quote: avenues to ban fracking everywhere in the county should be explored
statements.claim: Supports a county-land fracking ban, exploring wider restrictions, ending what he calls pay-to-pollute practices and investing in cleaner transport. Exploration is not represented as an already enacted countywide ban.

statements.quote: our standards will have to become increasingly stringent
statements.claim: Calls for enforcement and stronger industrial-pollution standards, working with the health department toward a greener economy.

statements.quote: low-income residents are protected
statements.claim: Supports reassessment, transparent processes and education, with protections against displacement of low-income residents.

statements.quote: a more transparent and equitable manner
statements.claim: Calls for a major assessment-system overhaul through a council committee with broader participation. The answer does not specify every new valuation rule.

statements.quote: More staff and resources are needed for County Council
statements.claim: Supports greater council staffing and resources to advance policy and constituent priorities.

statements.quote: We do need help.
statements.claim: Says limited staffing impedes council's serious oversight and deliberative responsibilities and calls for more help.

statements.quote: We must put a moratorium on hyperscale data centers
statements.claim: Supports a moratorium until strong safeguards are enacted, ending tax exemptions and NDAs, and holding operators responsible for environmental and utility burdens.

statements.quote: Yes. We cannot allow any infrastructure to be built that poses a danger
statements.claim: Supports the proposed moratorium and emphasizes water, ratepayer and climate safeguards.

statements.quote: During this 5 year moratorium
statements.claim: Supports a five-year moratorium to study environmental, water and utility-rate impacts.

statements.quote: I’ll do the same at the state level.
statements.claim: Proposes a statewide moratorium modeled on the Madison measure she says she sponsored, with guardrails and local input. Her claimed exclusivity is not independently endorsed.

statements.quote: I not only support a moratorium on hyperscale data centers
statements.claim: Supports a moratorium and repeal of the tax credit subsidizing data-center projects.

statements.quote: We’ll legalize rent control
statements.claim: Supports restoring the legal ability to regulate rents, along with shifting data-center tax subsidies toward housing.

statements.quote: repealing the bans on rent stabilization
statements.claim: Supports restoring local rent-stabilization and inclusionary-zoning authority, alongside a Tenant Bill of Rights.

statements.quote: use the $2 billion in tax breaks for data centers to build homes instead
statements.claim: Proposes redirecting data-center tax benefits toward housing, re-legalizing rent control and changing school finance to ease property taxes. Fiscal totals and projected effects remain campaign claims.

statements.quote: allow for single-stairway buildings
statements.claim: Proposes dense-housing incentives, building-code changes and investment in condos, duplexes and cooperatives.

statements.quote: Keep investment local. Build more rental housing.
statements.claim: Would curb outside private-equity and hedge-fund purchases, retain local investment and build more rental homes.

statements.quote: ease the restrictions on the $500 million dollar housing fund
statements.claim: Proposes easier access to WHEDA housing funds and surplus-funded housing grants. The separate near-duplicate public-bank answer is not used as independent evidence here.

statements.quote: raise our minimum wage to $23/hr
statements.claim: Proposes a $23 minimum wage indexed to living costs. No opponent's lower preferred wage is inferred from a less specific answer.

statements.quote: experience in all levels of government
statements.claim: Presents local, federal-liaison and state legislative work, along with a named tax proposal, as distinguishing qualifications. The assertion that she alone has this experience is not independently certified.

statements.quote: I’ve lived the policy failures of our state government.
statements.claim: Presents a nontraditional background and lived experience of policy failures as a perspective missing from the legislature.

statements.quote: creating a Badgercare public option
statements.claim: Proposes a BadgerCare public option; the questionnaire does not support labeling this candidate indifferent to public healthcare.

statements.quote: legalize marijuana completely for recreational and medicinal use
statements.claim: Supports recreational and medical cannabis legalization and argues that revenues could help fund education.

comparisons.analysis: Both support public housing. Gross emphasizes expanding public and collective ownership; Botta specifies short- and medium-term public housing with other tenant measures. Shared support does not imply identical delivery models.
Both support inclusionary zoning. Gross invokes neighborhood mandates and says the tool is insufficient alone; Botta calls for citywide coverage. No Gross opposition to expansion is inferred.
Both support public investment in youth and community services as violence prevention, while naming different programs and levels of funding.

Gross proposes civilianizing duties that need not be done by officers; Botta emphasizes staffing, retention, pay and wellness. These measures can coexist and neither answer establishes opposition to every other intervention.
Both explicitly oppose privatizing Shuman and want public accountability. The DSA endorsement is not evidence of an exclusive commitment to public ownership.

McDermott specifies wider fracking restrictions and clean transport; Klein stresses enforcing and strengthening pollution standards. The absence of a Klein fracking commitment here is not coded as opposition.
Both want a more equitable assessment system. McDermott specifies reassessment and protection against low-income displacement; Klein stresses a participatory committee-led overhaul.
Both say council needs greater staff or resources. McDermott foregrounds advancing policy; Klein foregrounds oversight and deliberative responsibilities.
Both support a hyperscale data-center moratorium and public safeguards; their details do not establish identical eventual permitting rules.
Both support a moratorium. Castañeda specifies five years for study; Bennett ties it to enactment of safeguards. The shared position does not erase those timing conditions.
Both support a statewide moratorium and stronger safeguards. Martinez-Rutherford also emphasizes local control and her stated record in Madison.
Both support a moratorium and ending tax advantages for data-center development.
Both support restoring the ability to regulate rents. Martinez-Rutherford additionally names local inclusionary-zoning authority and a Tenant Bill of Rights.
Bennett emphasizes reallocating tax benefits, rent control and school-finance/property-tax changes; Ben-Ami emphasizes density and building-code reform. These are potentially complementary measures.
Bennett emphasizes tax reallocation and rent regulation; Castañeda emphasizes constraining outside investors and constructing more rentals. Neither answer establishes rejection of the other's tools.

Bennett names tax reallocation and rent regulation; Sullivan names housing-fund access and grants. Their separate near-duplicate public-bank responses are withheld from independent comparison pending attribution review.

Here the DSA-endorsed candidate emphasizes experience inside several levels of government, while another Democrat emphasizes a nontraditional background and lived policy failures. The usual insider-versus-outsider shorthand cannot be assigned from endorsement labels alone.
